summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for carrying ITU Recommendation BT.656-3 video streams. It lets this kind of digital video be sent in real time over IP. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It says how to cut up a certain kind of digital video into packets for sending, and how to glue the packets back together at the other end.

subtitle: How to send studio-quality uncompressed BT.656 digital video over RTP, one scan line at a time.

tldr.problem: Uncompressed studio digital video (ITU BT.656-3) has no standard way to ride on RTP, and packets can be lost or reordered, so each packet needs enough information to place itself in the picture.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries all or part of one scan line, behind a four-octet payload header holding field, vertical-interval, type, quantization, scan line number and scan offset. Timing codes and line blanking are dropped and the receiver regenerates them.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can rebuild a BT.656 stream from packets that each stand alone, at the cost of roughly 20 megabytes per second of bandwidth.

today: RFC 2431 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 1998, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RTP as described in RFC 1889.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2431 describes how to packetize uncompressed, studio-quality video streams defined by ITU-R Recommendation BT.656-3 for transport over the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP). BT.656 is a way to interconnect digital television equipment on 525-line or 625-line standards, using the 4:2:2 encoding parameters of BT.601-5.

A full RTP specification for an application needs the RTP protocol document, a profile document and a payload format specification. This RFC is the payload format specification for studio-quality video.
sections.eli5: RTP is a delivery truck for live media. This RFC says how to pack one very high-quality kind of video onto the truck.

sections.title: Samples and Definitions
sections.content: The RFC defines a few terms. Y is an 8-bit or 10-bit coded luminance sample with 220 quantization levels, where black is level 16 and peak white is 235. Cb and Cr are coded color-difference samples with 225 quantization levels in the centre of the scale, where a color-difference of zero is encoded as 128. True Black is the quad-sample sequence 0x80, 0x10, 0x80, 0x10. SAV and EAV are timing reference codes at the start and end of a BT.656 scan line.
sections.eli5: Each dot of the picture is described by how bright it is and what color tint it has. True black is a special set of numbers meaning a dark, empty line.

sections.title: Payload Design
sections.content:
The format requires 4:2:2 subsampling, so luminance takes twice the bandwidth of each color-difference stream. For a normal 4:3 image that gives 720 luminance samples per line, 360 samples of each of the two chrominance channels, and 1440 samples in total. Only sizes and frame rates in accordance with BT.601-5 are currently supported. With no compression the stream can need approximately 20 megabytes per second of network bandwidth.

Each scan line is sent in one or more packets. The SAV and EAV codes and the line blanking samples are removed, so no ancillary data can be carried in line blanking. The receiver generates the timing codes and inserts the right number of blanking samples. Frame blanking samples are optional; if present (for example VITC or teletext data) they MUST be copied unmodified into the resulting stream, and if absent the receiver MUST generate true black levels.

Scan lines MUST be sent in sequential order, and error concealment for missing data is up to the receiver. Both 8-bit and 10-bit quantization are supported. A 10-bit sample has two extra bits of fixed-point precision, so binary 10111110.11 is 190.75, which is 190 in 8 bits. Applications SHOULD attempt path MTU discovery and fragment lines to fit. Fragmentation MUST fall on a sample-pair boundary: four-octet alignment for 8-bit and five-octet alignment for 10-bit samples.
sections.eli5: Because the video is not squashed, it is big. Each line is cut into pieces that fit in a packet, and the receiver fills in the blank parts itself.

sections.title: RTP Header Use and the Payload Header
sections.content:
Every packet has the normal RTP header, then a fixed four-octet payload header, then payload data. Three RTP header fields matter. The Marker bit is 1 on the last packet of a frame (the last fragment of the last scan line) and 0 otherwise. The Payload Type may be assigned by a profile, statically or dynamically. The Timestamp is the sampling instant of the frame, is the same for every scan line packet of that frame, and uses a 90kHz clock.

The payload header fields are:

  • F (1 bit): 0 for the first field of a frame, 1 for the second.
  • V (1 bit): 1 when the line is in the vertical interval; normally 0 unless frame blanking data is sent.
  • Type (4 bits): the frame encoding. It MUST stay the same for all lines of a frame.
  • P (1 bit): 0 for 8-bit samples, otherwise 10-bit samples. It also stays fixed within a frame.
  • Z (2 bits): reserved, set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
  • Scan Line (12 bits): the line number, valid values 1 through 625.
  • Scan Offset (11 bits): the sample-pair offset within the line, zero for the first packet of a line. For a 720-sample line the maximum is 359.

If a receiver builds a BT.656-3 stream directly, it MUST copy F and V from the header rather than deriving them from the line number; on conflict the F and V bits win.
sections.eli5: Every packet wears a small name tag: which half of the picture, which line number, and how far along the line this piece starts.

sections.title: Payload Data Layout
sections.content:
Following BT.656, each pair of color-difference samples is mixed with two luminance samples, and the order sent SHALL be Cb, Y, Cr, Y. A 720-sample line with 8-bit samples runs from Cb0, Y0, Cr0, Y1 up to Cb359, Y718, Cr359, Y719. Packets for 1144 and 1152 samples SHOULD grow accordingly with the same order.

For 10-bit quantization, each group of four samples MUST be encoded into a 40-bit word of five octets, in the same order. Octets are sent in network byte order, left to right as drawn.
sections.eli5: Brightness and color numbers are lined up in a fixed pattern, like beads on a string, so the receiver always knows which bead is which.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Packets in this format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification. Confidentiality of the media is achieved by encryption, and because the payload format is arranged end-to-end, encryption MAY be performed after encapsulation without conflict. The RFC also notes that this payload type has no significant non-uniformity in receiver processing cost that could create a denial-of-service threat.
sections.eli5: To keep the video private, lock the packets after they are packed. The packing itself does not give attackers an easy way to overload the receiver.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The 4-bit Type field allows up to sixteen encodings, with twelve currently reserved. Since new BT.656 schemes are considered very unlikely, requests to extend the field MUST be vetted by IANA, and implementors SHOULD check the IANA repository for new definitions. A request must include the requestor's name and contact information, the reason, and references to standards such as an updated BT.656. If the new type would lessen security, the risk MUST be described. A Designated Expert reviews the application.
sections.eli5: There are only a few video types so far, with spare slots kept for later. A grown-up referee at IANA decides who gets a new slot.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: 0 for the first field of a frame, 1 for the second.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: 1 when the line is part of the vertical interval.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Frame encoding: NTSC, PAL or the high definition variants.

items.label: NTSC
items.desc: 13.5MHz sample rate; 720 samples per line; 60 fields per second; 525 lines per frame.

items.label: PAL
items.desc: 13.5MHz sample rate; 720 samples per line; 50 fields per second; 625 lines per frame.

items.label: High Definition NTSC
items.desc: 18MHz sample rate; 1144 samples per line; 60 fields per second; 525 lines per frame.

items.label: High Definition PAL
items.desc: 18MHz sample rate; 1152 samples per line; 50 fields per second; 625 lines per frame.
